Features

Source: vignettes/articles/features.Rmd
features.Rmd

This is the full inventory, organised around the three independent axes the front page introduces — the bricks a system is described with, the time and space it is resolved on, and the route it is solved by — followed by what happens after a solve. Functions named here are exported; items marked (experimental) work but may change shape before 1.0. What changed in a release is in the release notes.

Bricks: describing a system

Component classes. commodity, supply, demand, technology, storage, trade, weather, constraint, tax, subsidy, costs, plus import / export for flows across the model boundary. Each is built by its newX() constructor, carries its data in slots, and is edited with update(), which derives a variant instead of re-typing the object.

  • Technologies convert any number of input commodities into any number of outputs, with conversion given per commodity (ceff), per group of commodities (@group), or as process activity (cap2act); availability by timeslice (af), by summed slices (afs) and per commodity (afc); ramping limits; capacity and retirement bounds; investment, fixed and variable costs.
  • Auxiliary flows (@aux / @aeff) couple a process’s capacity, new capacity, retirement, activity or any of its flows to a further commodity — land per MW, water per MWh, an emission per unit of fuel. They sit at the auxiliary commodity’s own timeframe, so an annual emission of an hourly plant is one variable per year.
  • Storage is three parts — charger, reservoir, discharger — each with its own capacity variable (vStorageInpCap, vStorageStgCap, vStorageOutCap), costs and availability. @duration sets reservoir hours per unit of discharge power, @inp2out the charger/discharger ratio and @inp2stg the charging C-rate; @seff holds charge, discharge and self-discharge efficiency; @startLevel the initial state. A storage may store one commodity and charge or discharge another.
  • Trade carries a commodity between regions on declared routes, with efficiency, capacity, costs, availability and lifetime. newACLine() and newDCLink() wrap the two common electrical cases; lossTranches() approximates quadratic losses by capacity tranches; an opt-in Kirchhoff voltage law constrains loop flows.
  • Weather supplies an exogenous time series that multiplies a process’s availability — capacity factors, inflows, a charging window. One series can serve many processes, be declared at a coarser region than its users, and derive further series through registered transforms (register_weather_transform()).
  • Policy objects. A constraint writes an arbitrary linear restriction over declared summands; tax and subsidy levy on a commodity total or on a named process; costs adds a user-defined cost term to the objective.
  • Commodity properties. @property carries physical data (heating values, densities, carbon content) as a tidy table; @emis emission factors; @agg aggregation into reporting groups; @limtype the balance direction.
  • Units are declared on flows and capacities, with cap2act making the capacity-to-activity conversion explicit, and getUnits() reporting what a model carries.
  • Portable definitions. process_to_spec() / process_from_spec() write and read a process as YAML or JSON; process_spec_issues() lints one; process_designer() is an interactive Shiny editor; read_technology_xlsx() / write_technology_xlsx() round-trip through Excel.

Variants and graded resources

  • Two axes on one object. @vintage declares build years with their investment window and operational life; @cluster declares parallel members that exist simultaneously — site grades, fleet types, tranches. Interpolation expands them into ordinary processes (EWIN_VIN2030_CL01), so every equation stays as it is.
  • Per-member data. Every parameter slot carries vintage and cluster columns; a row leaving them NA broadcasts to all members. A roster must be declared before a label may be used, which turns a typo into an error rather than a phantom member built from defaults.
  • Region-scoped members. @cluster$region scopes a member, so a tier set of a different size in each region is one object.
  • Family-level bounds. cap.share.fx and act.share.lo/up/fx bound how a family splits between its members; "TOTAL" in a selector column bounds the family as a whole.
  • Graded resources. A commodity declaring @cluster becomes one commodity per tier, each with its own balance, so grades cannot pool; a weather object declaring @cluster becomes one series per tier. Consumers resolve their tier by cluster name; unclustered objects are untouched.
  • Supply curves. asSupplyCurve(), asImportCurve() and asExportCurve() turn a single price into a stepped curve with its own roster.
  • Reading a family back. getVariants() (on a scenario or, before interpolating, on a model), getData(variants = TRUE) and variantSummary() — the provenance table is authoritative, so names are never parsed.

Axis one: time

  • User-defined nested calendars from timescales: the modeller states the hierarchy (ANNUAL > SEASON > DAY > HOUR, or whatever the question needs), the timeslices and their durations. There is no fixed 8,760-slice ceiling and no built-in assumption about what a “slice” is.
  • Mixed timeframes in one model. Each commodity balances at its own timeframe, so an annual fuel market, a seasonal reservoir and an hourly power balance coexist; a process may be declared coarser than the commodities it touches, and the equations aggregate.
  • Shipped designs. calendars carries generic layouts — m12, q4, s4_h24, d365_h24 and sampled variants such as d365_h24_1dps (one representative day per month) and s4_h24_subset_2seasons.
  • Sampled calendars. A model declared on a full calendar can be interpolated and solved on a subset of its slices, with annual quantities kept on a full-year basis — the usual way to iterate quickly and confirm at full resolution before reporting.
  • Horizons with uneven milestone years, interval weights and display labels (newHorizon()), and a calendar anchored to a year_start and a UTC offset.
  • Conversions and layout come from the sibling package: make_timetable(), tsl_sets(), autoplot() on a calendar, and the timescales API for label conversion.

Axis two: space

  • Nested geography from geoscales: a Geoscale describes how regions nest (nation > zone > node), attached with setGeoscale() or newModel(geoscale = ).
  • Multi-level balances. A commodity declares the level it balances on, so a national fuel market and nodal electricity live in one model without a trade route for every pair; coarse balances roll up.
  • Coarse processes. A technology or storage may sit at a level coarser than a commodity it uses, with its flows aggregated to the level where the balance is written.
  • Region aggregation. aggregate_model_regions() merges regions, including clusters = to partition a corridor family into k groups; get_process_groups() reports what may be merged, process_cluster_sweep() sweeps the admissible range of k, and model_clusters() reports what an aggregation did.
  • Sub-territory solves. A filtered geoscale handed to interpolate_model() solves part of a model’s territory; subset_model_regions() samples regions and warns when a sample splits a cell a process spans.
  • Maps. plot_geoscale(), plot_map() for any solved variable carrying a region, plot_trade_map() and plot_trade_network() for flows.

Axis three: the solve route

Four modelling languages, one direct-matrix route, and remote execution. The model definition does not change between them.

Route What it writes Notes
GLPK / MathProg .mod + .dat, solved by glpsol The transparent default. The glpsol R package bundles the binary on every platform and is used first when installed, so a first model needs no system solver
Julia / JuMP JuMP code for HiGHS, CBC, GLPK, CPLEX, cuOpt The usual choice for mid-size and large models
Python / Pyomo Pyomo for HiGHS, CBC, GLPK, CPLEX; MPS output For Python-based solver stacks
GAMS GAMS for CPLEX, CBC and others For institutional GAMS workflows
multimod (experimental) A language-neutral AST → LaTeX, backend code, or a direct LP/MPS matrix lang = "mm" skips the symbolic model build
  • Presets, not flags. solver_options carries named presets per backend — barrier, simplex, PDLP, crossover on or off, tolerances — including the first-order CPU preset julia_highs_pdlp and the GPU presets julia_cuopt and mm_cuopt_wsl.
  • GPU solving. NVIDIA cuOpt runs through JuMP on Linux, or on Windows through WSL (mm_cuopt_wsl), and on cloud hardware (mm_cuopt_cloud) through the experimental route below. See Solver backends for setup and the validation required before a first-order solution is trusted.
  • Remote execution. NEOS runs supported solver jobs without a local licence; the (experimental) cloud presets (mm_cuopt_cloud, pyomo_cuopt_cloud) ship the problem to cloud hardware through mmcloud, stream progress and retrieve the solution.
  • Solutions from elsewhere. read_solution() decodes a solution produced outside energyRt, so a model written here can be solved anywhere and read back.
  • Toolchain checks. en_setup(), en_check_dependencies(), en_check_packages(), en_install_deps(), en_install_julia_pkgs(), and en_check_solve(), which solves a tiny model on every configured backend and reports what actually works.

Generating the model

  • interpolate_model() resolves declarations into solver-ready parameters: interpolating over years, expanding variants, materialising tiers and weather transforms, building sets and mappings, and checking the result.
  • The model it writes has about 185 equation blocks over 93 variables (as written in glpk/energyRt.mod), extendable with newConstraint().
  • Sparse or dense, folded or explicit: sparse = drops rows equal to a default, fold = collapses dimensions that do not vary (region, timeslice, year), both losslessly.
  • On-disk interpolation writes parameters to an Arrow store, so a model too large for memory still builds.
  • Performance and transparency. The release notes record interpolation about six times faster than the 0.8 series on a 41-node hourly case, and every call appends per-stage and per-map timings to a log.
  • Model inspection. model_size() / size(), summary(), find_in_model(), findData(), findDuplicates(), audit_coefficients() for the written coefficient ranges, and compare_inputs() to diff two interpolated models.

Solve strategies

  • solve_model() — the whole pipeline, or the verbs separately (interpolate_model(), write_script(), read_solution()).
  • solve_myopic() — window by window with limited foresight, built on an exported solution ledger (solution_ledger(), apply_ledger(), horizon_windows(), myopic_objective()).
  • solve_by_sample() — one solve per sampled calendar (calendar_samples(), sample_summary()).
  • solve_by_region() — regional decomposition with boundary windows.
  • solve_guided() — iterate toward a target (solution_targets(), apply_targets(), guided_gap()).
  • Every driver records its runs under the scenario, with the parameters it was called with.

Scenarios, storage and provenance

  • A project registry keyed on path records models, repositories, scenarios and datasets: newRegistry(), load_registry(), refresh_registry(), add_to_registry(), and summary() for counts and staleness. Objects are reachable by name — getScenario("base"), getObject() — so a study with thousands of solved runs stays addressable.
  • Lifecycle. seal_model() / unseal_*() freeze an entry as a version; only sealed versions are referenced. list_versions() lists the versions of models, repositories and datasets with their status; mark_delete() and delete_marked() stage removals and refuse to break a reference; list_dependents() says what points at an object.
  • Scenarios built on a base. interpolate_model(..., base = REF) reuses an interpolated scenario’s tables for a scenario that adds constraints, costs, levies, processes or commodities, or samples REF’s calendar or regions; the result equals a full interpolation. On a sealed REF, the saved scenario references REF’s tables instead of copying them.
  • Runs and artefacts. scenario_runs(), scenario_solutions(), scenario_artifacts() report what each solve produced and left on disk; promote_solution() and import_solution() choose which solution counts; drop_solver_outputs() and drop_scenario_run() clean up; upgrade_scenario_layout() migrates older folders.
  • Arrow-backed results. Solutions and inputs live in Parquet/Arrow stores with lazy reading, so results larger than memory stay usable; isInMemory() / isOnDisk() / obj2mem() move between the two.
  • Hashes and reproducibility. model_hash(), repository_hash(), dataset_hash(), object_hash(); an optional operation log (set_log_file()); run.yml recording a solve’s memory footprint and timings.
  • Sharing. prepare_for_sharing() writes a cleaned, trimmed copy of a stored scenario; strip_user_info() removes the machine it was built on.

Results and analysis

  • getData() returns tidy data for any parameter or variable, with merge = TRUE for set labels, variants = TRUE for provenance, interpolate = TRUE for the interpolated series, run = to read several runs at once, and timeframe = to aggregate.
  • get_variable(), getMix() (with top_n lumping), get_weather(), read_sequence() for a driver’s sequence of solves.
  • Levelized cost. levcost() prices a technology, a storage (LCOS) or a trade route (LCOT) analytically — no solver — per vintage, cluster and region, from either a declared object or a solved scenario; results are cached on disk. tech_share_frontier() and plot_share_frontier() show how the merit order shifts with a share constraint.
  • Comparison. compare_scenarios() (solved results, or runs of one scenario), compare_models() (declarations) and compare_inputs() (interpolated inputs), each with an autoplot() method.
  • Decomposition drivers sum by region and average by sample, so a multi-run study aggregates correctly.

Validation and diagnostics

  • validate_scenario_parameters() separates structural findings — the model would solve to a meaningless answer — from advisory ones, and names them: a populated flow with no capacity link (free_meal), constraint tuples with no data behind them, coefficient ranges that will hurt a solver, duplicate keys, and variant provenance that disagrees with the process names.
  • verify_solution() re-derives the model’s own identities from the results — balances, capacity limits, storage dynamics, emissions, costs — with check groups (checks = "all") and verify_checks() listing them.
  • audit_coefficients() reports coefficient ranges per equation of a written model, which is where a scaling problem shows up before the solver struggles.
  • Structural refusals at build time: an undeclared weather link, a geoscale whose levels do not nest, a commodity finer than the process producing it, a variant name colliding with an existing object, a tier a consumer asks for but the resource does not declare.
  • en_check_dependencies() / en_check_packages() for the environment, and trim_parameters() / update_parameter() for surgery on an interpolated model.

Visualisation and reporting

  • Diagrams. draw() sketches a process’s flow structure — inputs, outputs, auxiliary flows, groups, and a storage’s three parts with their ratio couplings.
  • autoplot() on objects (declared data as points, interpolated as lines), calendars, horizons, levelized costs, comparisons, and solved scenarios (type = "generation", "capacity", "new_capacity", "fuel", "storage", with by = "vintage" / "cluster" fan-outs, faceting and top_n).
  • Maps — see the space axis above — and plot_heatmap() for a timeslice × region view.
  • Reports. report() renders any energyRt object — fourteen element classes plus the model, repository and scenario containers — to HTML, PDF, Word or TeX. Reports are cached, follow user-defined process groups, carry branding (misc$logos, misc$badges), and are built from an exported report_* helper family so a template can be replaced. report_templates() lists what ships.
  • theme_energyRt(), object_image() and design() for consistent styling.

Interoperability

  • multimod turns an interpolated scenario into a language-neutral model — multimod_from_energyRt() — from which it renders LaTeX, emits code for other modelling languages, or assembles the LP matrix directly without the symbolic model-build step that can dominate time and memory on large problems. multimod_import_data() and multimod_unmatched() bring results and diagnostics back.
  • OSeMOSYS / TIMES conventions are followed where they exist — the timeslice dimension, the parameter naming style — so a model is legible to users of those frameworks.
  • The sibling stack: timescales (time), geoscales (space), nestedscales (the nested-set core these two are built on), glpsol (the bundled GLPK binary) and mmcloud (remote execution).
  • Tidy in, tidy out: everything crosses the boundary as a data frame, so the usual tidyverse and arrow tooling applies.

Learning and examples

  • TOPIA, the packaged teaching model: a multi-region power system built up step by step over three articles (build, run scenarios, multi-level regions), with scenario levers (CO2 cap, carbon tax, renewable share, no new nuclear, early retirement) and add-on modules.
  • Unit kits (topia$modules$unit): minimal models whose every input is an integer, so the objective can be computed by hand — the fastest way to check a backend or a change.
  • Articles for installation, backends, model bricks, units, time and space resolution, storage, vintages and clusters, workflow, scenario management, reports and autoplot().
  • A production example. IDEEA applies the same machinery to India’s power system at full resolution.

Engineering

  • A tiered test suite — check < fast < cross < full — with a coverage matrix tying tests to the model entities they exercise (@covers), tracked goldens for interpolated inputs and solved results, cross-backend equivalence tests, and a backend probe that skips what the machine cannot solve.
  • Deterministic builds. data-raw/ drivers are idempotent; bundled datasets are regenerated rather than hand-edited.
  • Apache-2.0 licensed, with the sibling packages under the same terms.
